# Sāleyyaka Sutta (MN 41 (PTS MN i 285))
**ID:** MN 41 (PTS MN i 285)

**Title (Pali):** Sāleyyaka Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sāleyyaka Sutta* (MN 41) is the forty-first discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, positioned within the *Cūḷayamakavagga* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The discourse is set in the Kosalan brahmin village of Sālā, where the Buddha addresses a large gathering of brahmin householders (*brāhmaṇagahapatikā*) concerning the moral causes governing rebirth in favorable or unfavorable destinies [McTighe; Hazra 1994; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha explicates the ten courses of action (*kammapatha*), contrasting unwholesome and wholesome conduct across three bodily deeds (killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct / *kāmesu micchācāra*), four verbal deeds (such as false witness in assemblies versus truthful speech), and three mental deeds (covetousness, ill will, and wrong view versus their wholesome counterparts) [Farrington; Rogell 2003; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Thanissaro Bhikkhu 2013]. He further describes how righteous conduct, combined with specific mental aspiration, leads to rebirth across twenty-five celestial planes—spanning the sense-sphere heavens (*kāmaloka*), subtle form realms (*rūpaloka*), and formless realms (*arūpaloka*)—or ultimately to liberation through the destruction of the taints [Hazra 1994; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Sagaraghosa 2011; SuttaCentral].
Within the Pali canon, the discourse is virtually identical in content to the *Verañjaka Sutta* (MN 42), which repeats its doctrinal exposition nearly verbatim for a different audience [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Anālayo 2018]. Other major Pali parallels and text-reuse partners include AN 10.176 (sharing large segments detailing the ten courses of action), AN 2.6, AN 3.28, and MN 114 (*Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta*) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. The sutta is cited or referenced in canonical and paracanonical treatises including the *Niddesa* (Mnd 7, Mnd 14, Cnd 22) and the *Puggalapaññatti* (Pp 2.3) [SuttaCentral]. Chinese parallels are preserved in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ 1042 and SĀ 1043) [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Anālayo 2018]. Comparative study reveals that while the Pali text subdivides the Brahmā and radiant heavens (*ābhā*, *subhā*), its Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* counterpart lists only the primary heavenly spheres, reflecting a Theravāda editorial tendency toward more elaborate cosmological taxonomies [Nattier; Anālayo 2018]. DharmaNexus also aligns its treatment of rebirth and deeds with Sanskrit and Tibetan scholastic texts, including the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and the *Karmaprajñapti* [DharmaNexus].
